analysis.one_liner: Caps donations from out-of-state donors at $100, bans PAC money, and restricts party and corporate political spending.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the House Administration Committee, and never received a vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal campaign finance rules in four ways: it would cap contributions from people who cannot vote in a state or district at $100 (instead of $1,000), ban candidates from taking money from political action committees, require corporations and unions to get separate written permission before using shareholder or member money for politics, and ban the unlimited 'soft money' contributions that national parties could otherwise raise outside federal limits.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters in a congressional district, who would see candidates relying more on their own small contributions rather than money from PACs, out-of-district donors, and unlimited party accounts. Shareholders and union members would also gain control over whether their money funds political activity.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters outspent by PACs and big donors

how_it_helps.text: Caps contributions to a House or Senate candidate at $100 per person from anyone not eligible to vote in that state or district, down from the $1,000 general limit, so local voters' voices are not drowned out by money from elsewhere [S2] [S3].
Bans candidates for federal office from accepting any contribution from a nonparty political action committee [S2] [S3].

Bars corporations, national banks, and labor unions from using dues or assessments for political activity without a separate prior written voluntary authorization from each individual, and requires corporations to get shareholder approval of pro-rata shares of planned political spending before each 12-month period [S2] [S3].

Bans national political parties and federal candidates from soliciting, receiving, or spending soft money not subject to federal limits, requires state parties to fund mixed activities like voter registration drives only from federally regulated accounts, and blocks transfers of unregulated funds between state parties [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees, national party committees that relied on soft money, and corporations and unions whose pooled political spending would need individual written approval would all lose funding channels; campaigns would have to rebuild their fundraising around individual donors.
analysis.who_pays_short: PACs, party committees, corporations, and unions

drawbacks.text: The shareholder and member authorization rules impose a large administrative burden: corporations would have to mail annual notices with pro-rata calculations and collect approval forms before every 12-month period, and unions argue opt-in requirements let dues-payers free ride on collective political activity [S3].

Banning PAC contributions while leaving independent expenditures untouched could push money out of disclosed, regulated channels and into less accountable forms of spending, a longstanding criticism of contribution-ban approaches [S3].

The tight contribution limits only apply to money given to candidates; independent and party spending outside those channels would remain, so the bill restricts one funding path without addressing the total amount of money in elections [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks several channels of concentrated political money at once, and the cost of doing so falls on the political fundraising operations of PACs, parties, corporations, and unions rather than on ordinary people. Its real weaknesses are design gaps: the individual permission requirements create substantial paperwork, unions would see their pooled political voice sharply reduced, and independent spending remains untouched. On balance it would have meaningfully limited big-money influence in congressional elections, though not eliminated it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee in February 1999 and sat there without action until the Congress ended in January 2001, never reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Campbell introduced the Can't Vote, Can't Contribute Campaign Reform Act of 1999 on February 11, 1999 [S1] [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration [S2] [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point [S4].

No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing reported in the record, was never reported out of committee, and never received a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the political fundraising machinery around them — PACs, national party committees, and corporate and union political funds — kept the existing channels open because the bill never advanced; no restrictions took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents and existing campaign money channels

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors joined the Republican sponsor and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no party breakdown to measure.

industries.note: The bill bans all PAC contributions to federal candidates, eliminating the PAC funding channel entirely. Their gain from the bill's failure is continued access to candidates that ordinary donors cannot match [S3].

The bill bans national parties from raising or spending soft money outside federal limits and tightens state party funding rules. Parties would lose the unlimited money they use for voter drives and advertising [S3].

Corporate political spending would require prior written authorization from each shareholder and annual pro-rata approval, sharply limiting corporate political funds. Their interest in the status quo runs against voters who cannot match corporate money [S3].

Union political use of dues would require separate written authorization from each member and could be revoked anytime. Unions would lose pooled political spending, a burden unions view as disproportionate even as some members would gain individual control over their dues [S3].
